finding.claim: Authorization check on /admin/drop is computed and discarded, so any authenticated user can reach the DROP TABLE path.
finding.source: Any authenticated caller. The user comes from the request context via userFrom (api.go:22), and roles are only checked via Authorize.
finding.sink: Protected operation at api.go:27 (runSQL DROP TABLE) and the DBA-only route registered at api.go:44.

trace.note: /admin/drop is routed to dropTable with no middleware or role check in this file.
u := userFrom(r) takes the user from request context.
Authorize(u, "dba") is called, but its error return is not checked. The code continues whether or not the user has the dba role.
runSQL executes the DROP TABLE regardless of authorization.

finding.guards_checked: Authorize itself is correct (api.go:13-20 returns an error when the role is missing). The bug is that its result is dropped, unlike vacuum (api.go:33-36), which returns on error. No role check, method check or CSRF protection appears in this file. The upstream middleware that sets the user is not in the reviewed code, so I could not confirm whether it adds a role gate.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize (api.go:13-20) does return an error, but its result is discarded as a bare statement at api.go:26, so it blocks nothing. The route at api.go:44 has no middleware or role check. The vacuum handler (api.go:33-36) checks the error correctly, but that is a different route. The directory contains only api.go, so no upstream middleware that adds a role gate is present in the repo.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: userFrom at api.go:25, the discarded Authorize result at api.go:26, and the unconditional runSQL("DROP TABLE " + r.FormValue("t")) at api.go:27, routed without a role gate at api.go:44, so any authenticated user reaches the drop. The candidate's "DBA-only route" wording is wrong, since nothing in the code restricts /admin/drop to DBAs; the only residual uncertainty is an external gateway outside this repo.

finding.claim: The table name from the request is concatenated into a DROP TABLE statement with no validation, so it is SQL injection.
finding.source: r.FormValue("t") at api.go:27. FormValue reads both query-string and form-body parameters, so the value is attacker-controlled.

trace.note: The attacker-controlled value from FormValue("t") is concatenated directly into the SQL string.
runSQL is a stub here. If it executes its argument as SQL, the input is injected verbatim.

finding.guards_checked: No allowlist, identifier quoting, length or character check. The table name cannot be parameterized, so it needs an allowlist of known table names. The F1 authorization gap means this is reachable by any authenticated user, not just DBAs. Impact is inferred from the function name, since runSQL is a stub in this code.

verdict.guard_found: None on the injection path. api.go:26 calls Authorize(u, "dba") but discards its error, so it is not a guard, and the route is reachable by any authenticated user. No parameterization, identifier quoting, or table-name allowlist exists between api.go:27 and the sink. Only api.go:13-20 defines Authorize, and only the vacuum handler at api.go:33 checks it.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: api.go:27 concatenates the attacker-controlled r.FormValue("t") into the SQL string with no allowlist, and the missing authorization at api.go:26 means any authenticated user can reach it. But runSQL at api.go:41 is an empty stub (`func runSQL(string) {}`), so the code provided never executes the string as SQL, and whether it is injectable depends on an implementation that is not present.
